title: Harvesting sunflower shoots
subtitle: When and how to cut, de-hull, rinse, and store sunflower microgreen shoots
excerpt: Sunflower shoots are ready when the large cotyledons are fully open, deep green, and 8 to 12 cm tall, around day 10 to 14. Cut 2 cm above the medium. Some cotyledons will have seed hulls attached; mist and wait before removing them. Store for up to two days refrigerated.
sourceNotes: UMass Extension microgreens guides (open-access). Cornell Cooperative Extension indoor growing material. Standard microgreen-growing practice synthesised from extension service material.

glossaryTerms.definition: The seed leaf — the first leaf or pair of leaves produced by a germinating seed. Sunflower cotyledons are much larger than brassica cotyledons: wide, flat, and substantial, with a slightly waxy surface. They are harvested as the edible shoot and have a mild, nutty flavour.

The process of removing the remaining seed hulls from sunflower cotyledons after the blackout phase. The heavy weight used during the blackout period causes most hulls to separate from the cotyledon as the shoot pushes up through the resistance. Remaining hulls can be removed by misting with water and waiting 20 to 30 minutes for the hull to soften.

content.text: Sunflower shoots are the most substantial of the common microgreen crops. The large, flat cotyledons are harvested when fully open and deep green, around day 10 to 14 from sowing. The harvest requires one extra step that smaller crops don't: dealing with any seed hulls still attached to the cotyledons.

should be fully flat and open (not still cupped or folded) and a deep even green. At full development, the cotyledons are 3 to 5 cm across and the shoot is 8 to 12 cm tall. Sunflower shoots at the right stage have a firm, slightly waxy texture.

The harvest window for sunflower is broader than for brassicas: quality holds for 2 to 3 days once the cotyledons are fully open. Harvest before the tiny true leaves appear at the centre of the cotyledons.
Before cutting: check for seed hulls still attached to the cotyledons.

: mist any remaining hulls with water and wait 20 to 30 minutes. The hulls soften and can be gently pinched off with your fingers. The cotyledon will not be damaged if the hull is removed when softened; trying to remove a dry, hard hull risks tearing the cotyledon.

Cutting: use clean scissors and cut 2 cm above the medium surface. The higher cut point (2 cm vs the standard 1 cm for brassicas) gives a longer stem and avoids the tougher base of the sunflower shoot. Work from one side of the tray to the other.

Rinse cut sunflower shoots in a colander under cold water. Check once more for any remaining hull fragments and remove them. Shake out excess water. Refrigerate in a sealed container with a dry kitchen paper lining for up to two days.

attrs.heading: Troubleshooting
attrs.intro: Common harvest-stage problems with sunflower shoots.

items.symptom: Many hulls still firmly attached to cotyledons at harvest time
items.cause: Insufficient blackout weight, or hull not fully softened by the pre-soak.
items.fix: Mist the hulls and wait 30 minutes before attempting to remove them. On the next batch, increase the blackout weight to 1.5 to 2 kg and ensure the pre-soak is a full 8 hours.

items.symptom: Cotyledons not fully flat even after day 14
items.cause: Insufficient light, or cover removed too early from the blackout phase.
items.fix: Move to a brighter position or increase grow-light duration. The cotyledons need 12 to 24 hours of bright light to open fully; check again the following day.

items.symptom: Cut stems turn slimy in the refrigerator within 24 hours
items.cause: Excess moisture in the storage container.
items.fix: Ensure kitchen paper lining is dry and replaced if it becomes saturated. Don't pile sunflower shoots in a deep container; the weight compresses the lower shoots.
